primitives.name: Market Pricing Edge Threshold
primitives.verbatim_quote: The real teaser decision is conditional on the pair you're teased together, and modern books price teasers at -125/-130 (breakeven ~48.3%/50% per leg), which eats most of the historical edge.
primitives.assumptions: Teaser pricing reflects bookmaker risk-adjusted expectations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When observed leg rates fall below breakeven threshold.

layer2.mapping: Informs GSI’s edge detection logic; GSE uses this to evaluate whether to enter teaser positions.
layer2.telemetry: Current teaser pricing vs. historical leg-cover thresholds.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight centers on the distinction between unconditional and conditional leg-cover probabilities. Unconditional rates (~67–77%) appear strong in isolation but fail to account for interdependence among legs in a teaser. The breakeven threshold (48.3%–50%) derived from modern pricing implies that even historically high rates may not yield positive EV. The mathematical duality lies in how the joint probability of two legs must exceed 45.45% for a -120 teaser to be profitable, yet real-world pairing effects often dilute this. This creates a failure mode where historical edge is eroded by market efficiency. The conditional nature of leg coverage introduces a non-trivial dependency structure that requires dynamic modeling. The key derivation involves transforming unconditional empirical rates into conditional expectations under fixed teaser payouts. This leads to a dualism: historical data suggests an exploitable edge, but current pricing reflects a corrected equilibrium. The epistemic challenge is distinguishing signal from noise in leg correlations, especially when data spans pre-2002 environments with differing total distributions.
